items.prompt: How did the huge shark Megalodon's teeth let it feed on prey as tough as whales?

options.label: The teeth were smooth-edged, built to grip and hold prey still
options.feedback: A smooth edge grips well but does not cut; teeth this size with a fine serrated edge were built for slicing through flesh, not just holding on.

options.label: The teeth were serrated like a saw and constantly replaced
options.feedback: Tiny saw-like ridges along each tooth's edge sliced through flesh and blubber, and any tooth broken or lost was simply replaced by another growing in behind it.

options.label: The teeth dissolved prey with acid before biting down
options.feedback: No shark's teeth carry or release acid; a bite works purely as a cutting and gripping tool.

options.label: The teeth were used only for digging in the seabed
options.feedback: Their shape — flat, wide, and edged like a blade — suits shearing through flesh, not scraping through sediment.

items.ok_line: A saw-edged blade with an endless supply behind it.
items.ko_line: Look at the edge of the tooth itself, and ask what happens when one breaks.
items.exp_title: A saw's edge, with replacements always ready
items.exp_text: Each tooth carried a fine row of serrations down its edge, turning it into a small saw rather than a smooth point, well suited to shearing through flesh and blubber as the jaw closed. Sharks of every kind lose teeth constantly to the stress of biting, and rows of replacements waiting behind the working teeth moved forward to take their place. A mouth armed this way kept a full set of cutting edges in service without ever depending on a single tooth surviving for long.

items.prompt: How did the giant snake Titanoboa most likely kill the prey it wrapped its coils around?

options.label: By crushing every bone in the prey's body
options.feedback: A constrictor's coils are strong, but killing works through the breath and blood, not by shattering a skeleton.

options.label: By biting once and injecting venom
options.feedback: Nothing about its jaw or teeth suggests venom delivery; the killing method associated with a snake this size and shape is constriction.

options.label: By tightening its coils a little more each time the prey breathed out
options.feedback: Each exhale gave the prey's chest a little more room, and the snake took up the slack immediately, so the chest could never expand again to draw in the next breath.

options.label: By holding the prey underwater until it drowned
options.feedback: Constriction does not depend on water at all; the coils do their work by squeezing, on land or in water alike.

items.ok_line: Tightening the coil after every breath out, until no breath could come back in.
items.ko_line: Think about what a constrictor does the instant its prey's chest gets a little smaller.
items.exp_title: Taking up the slack with every breath
items.exp_text: A constricting snake does not simply squeeze as hard as it can from the start; it tightens its coils gradually, taking up whatever small amount of room appears each time the prey's chest relaxes and shrinks slightly on breathing out. Prevented from expanding again, the chest cannot draw in a fresh breath, and blood flow to the brain is choked off along with it. Titanoboa's coils worked the same way, tightening a little further with every breath its prey let out, until breathing stopped for good.

items.prompt: How did a giant arthropod like Arthropleura, a metres-long relative of the millipede, manage to breathe without lungs?

options.label: It absorbed oxygen through its shell alone
options.feedback: A hard outer shell blocks gas exchange rather than allowing it; air had to reach the tissues by another route entirely.

options.label: It surfaced regularly to gulp air into an internal sac
options.feedback: No air sac of that kind is known in this animal; its breathing system worked through openings along the body instead.

options.label: Air entered through small openings along its body and travelled directly to the tissues in branching tubes
options.feedback: A network of fine tubes carried air from spiracles along the sides of the body straight to the tissues that needed it, without any lungs or blood involved.

options.label: It breathed only through its mouth, like a mammal
options.feedback: Mouth-breathing belongs to animals with lungs; this body plan moved air through a separate system of tubes opening along its sides.

items.ok_line: Air piped straight to the tissues, no lungs and no blood needed for the job.
items.ko_line: Insects and their relatives breathe through openings in the body wall, not through a mouth or a shell.
items.exp_title: Air delivered directly, tube by tube
items.exp_text: Along the sides of the body sat small openings called spiracles, each one leading into a branching network of fine tubes that carried air straight to the tissues that needed it, rather than relying on lungs and a bloodstream to move oxygen around. This kind of breathing works well because air has to diffuse through the tubes for a short distance to reach any given cell. Richer oxygen in the surrounding air let that same diffusion process deliver enough fuel to keep every tissue supplied, tube by tube, cell by cell.

items.prompt: How did the sabre-toothed cat Smilodon most likely use its long, curved canine teeth to kill prey?

options.label: By crushing through bone with a powerful bite, as a modern lion does
options.feedback: Long, blade-thin canines like these would snap under the stress of biting into bone; a modern lion's shorter, thicker teeth are shaped for that kind of force instead.

options.label: By using the canines only for display, never for killing
options.feedback: Wear patterns and occasional broken tips found on fossil canines show they were used hard against prey, not kept purely for show.

options.label: By using the canines to dig prey out of burrows
options.feedback: Blade-like canines this long and thin would fracture against packed earth; digging strains teeth in a way these were not built to withstand.

options.label: By gaping its jaw wide and driving the canines into a vulnerable spot such as the throat
options.feedback: An unusually wide gape let the jaw open far enough to clear the long canines, and a precise, stabbing bite to the throat or belly could kill without needing a bone-crushing grip.

items.ok_line: A wide-open jaw and a precise, stabbing strike, not a crushing grip.
items.ko_line: Ask how the jaw first had to open before those long canines could even be used.
items.exp_title: A stabbing bite from a wide-open jaw
items.exp_text: The canines were long, flattened, and edged rather than round and stout, a shape suited to slicing and stabbing rather than to withstanding the stress of crunching through bone. Powerful neck and shoulder muscles could pin struggling prey still while the jaw opened unusually wide to clear those long teeth, then drove them into a soft, vulnerable target such as the throat. A strike placed this precisely could kill quickly without ever putting the fragile canines at risk of the sideways forces that would snap them.

items.prompt: How did a long-necked plesiosaur most likely use its neck to catch fish?

options.label: By swimming its whole body directly at a fish shoal at high speed
options.feedback: A long, four-flippered body turns and accelerates slowly; the neck offered a faster, quieter way to strike than moving the whole body ever could.

options.label: By reaching the head out to snatch prey while the body stayed steady
options.feedback: A long neck let the head dart toward nearby prey while the broad, four-flippered body barely had to move, keeping the approach quiet until the strike itself.

options.label: By trailing the neck behind as a lure to attract fish
options.feedback: The neck led the head toward prey rather than trailing behind it; a trailing neck would put the head in the worst position to strike.

options.label: By coiling the neck around prey like a snake
options.feedback: A plesiosaur's neck, though long, was supported by a chain of stiffened vertebrae unsuited to coiling; it worked as a reaching, striking tool instead.

items.ok_line: A quiet body, and a neck that did the striking.
items.ko_line: Think about which part of the animal actually had to move fast to catch a fish, and which part could stay still.
items.exp_title: A body that hardly moves, a neck that strikes
items.exp_text: Four broad flippers rowed the plesiosaur's body through the water in a steady, controlled way, closer to flying underwater than to swimming with a tail. Approaching a shoal of fish this way disturbed the water far less than a fast, direct charge would, letting the animal come within reach without warning its prey. Once close enough, the long neck alone could dart the head forward at speed to seize a fish, while the rest of the body barely changed position at all.

items.prompt: How did a terror bird such as Phorusrhacos most likely use its huge hooked beak to kill prey?

options.label: By using it only to crack open seeds and nuts
options.feedback: A tall, hooked, blade-edged beak like this suits tearing flesh, not the blunt, rounded shape a seed-cracking beak needs.

options.label: By gripping prey gently and swallowing it whole
options.feedback: A beak built this heavy and sharp-edged was suited to striking and tearing, not to a gentle grip followed by swallowing without a struggle.

options.label: By delivering powerful, axe-like strikes down onto prey
options.feedback: A tall, narrow, hook-tipped beak driven downward with the neck's full strength could act like a hatchet, stunning or killing prey with repeated blows rather than a single crushing bite.

options.label: By spraying venom from a gland at the base of the beak
options.feedback: No venom delivery system is known in any bird living or extinct; a beak this shape and size did its killing by force alone.

items.ok_line: A beak swung like a hatchet, not clamped down like a jaw.
items.ko_line: Picture the beak's tall, narrow, hooked shape, and think of a tool with that same profile.
items.exp_title: A hatchet on the end of a long neck
items.exp_text: The beak was tall from top to bottom but narrow from side to side, ending in a sharp downward hook, a shape that concentrates force along a thin edge rather than spreading it the way a flatter, rounder beak would. Driven down by the strength of the neck, a strike like that could land like a blow from a hatchet, stunning or wounding smaller prey outright. Repeated strikes like this let the bird disable or kill prey using the beak alone, without needing a crushing, prolonged grip to finish the job.

items.prompt: How did a giant ground sloth such as Megatherium reach leaves high up in a tree, despite having no wings and a heavy body?

options.label: By climbing the trunk using its claws, the way a modern sloth does
options.feedback: A body this heavy would be far too much for a trunk to bear; instead it worked from the ground, using its own hind legs and tail as support.

options.label: By knocking the whole tree down before feeding
options.feedback: Skeletal evidence points to a controlled, upright reach rather than pushing trees over as a routine way of feeding.

options.label: By spitting a jet of water to knock leaves down
options.feedback: Nothing in this animal's build points to any water-spitting ability; height was gained by posture, not by any projectile.

options.label: By rearing up on its hind legs, using its tail as a third leg for support
options.feedback: A thick, muscular tail planted on the ground formed a stable tripod with the two hind legs, freeing the body to rise upright and stretch well above its own standing height.

items.ok_line: A tripod of two hind legs and a thick tail, freeing the body to stand tall.
items.ko_line: Think about what a heavy body needs on the ground before it can safely rise up on two legs.
items.exp_title: A tripod built from its own tail
items.exp_text: The tail was thick, muscular, and reinforced enough to bear real weight, unlike the thin tail of most ground-dwelling mammals. Planted against the ground alongside the two hind feet, it formed a stable tripod that could support the whole animal as it reared upright, freeing the long front claws to hook a branch and pull it within reach. Balanced this way on three points rather than two, a body far too heavy to climb could still feed on foliage well above where it normally stood.

items.prompt: How did the armour of a Glyptodon, an armadillo relative the size of a small car, actually protect it from predators?

options.label: Hundreds of separate bony plates fused together into one solid, curved shell
options.feedback: Individual plates of bone, called osteoderms, grew fused edge to edge into a single rigid dome over the back, spreading the force of any bite across the whole shell rather than one soft spot.

options.label: A layer of thick fur that absorbed the force of a bite
options.feedback: Fur alone cushions little against a determined predator's jaws; the real protection here came from bone, not hair.

options.label: A coating of venomous spines along the back
options.feedback: No venom-delivering spines are known on this animal; its defence came from a rigid shell of fused bone rather than any toxin.

options.label: Rapid burrowing underground the moment danger appeared
options.feedback: A body this bulky and heavily armoured was poorly built for fast digging; its main defence was the armour itself, not escape underground.

items.ok_line: One solid dome of bone, built from hundreds of plates fused together.
items.ko_line: Think about what the shell was actually made of, and how the pieces of it were joined.
items.exp_title: A dome built from fused bone
items.exp_text: Bony plates called osteoderms grew directly in the skin and fused together edge to edge, forming one continuous, curved shell rather than a set of loose scales. A shell rigid and unbroken like that spread the force of a bite or a blow out across its whole surface instead of letting it concentrate on any single weak point. Fused into one dome this way, the shell turned what would have been a killing bite anywhere on a softer-bodied animal into a blow the whole structure absorbed together.

items.prompt: How did the enormous hornless relative of the rhinoceros, Paraceratherium, reach food that other large plant-eaters of its time could not?

options.label: By using a long neck and long legs to browse treetop leaves, much as a giraffe does today
options.feedback: A neck and legs stretched well above other grazing animals let the head reach up into foliage far out of reach of anything feeding closer to the ground.

options.label: By using a long, flexible snout to pull down branches
options.feedback: Its build points to height doing the reaching rather than a grasping snout; the head itself was carried high enough to browse without needing one.

options.label: By digging up roots and tubers below the surface
options.feedback: A body built this tall, with long legs and a long neck, was suited to browsing high growth, not to digging down into the ground for buried food.

options.label: By knocking down trees to reach the canopy
options.feedback: Reaching upward through height, rather than bringing the canopy down to ground level, is what its long neck and legs were suited for.

items.ok_line: Height did the work that a trunk or a long snout does for other browsers.
items.ko_line: Think about what long legs and a long neck together let an animal reach, without any other tool involved.
items.exp_title: Reaching upward on long legs and a long neck
items.exp_text: Long legs raised the shoulders well above the animals grazing at ground level, and a long neck on top of that carried the head higher still, closer to the leaves growing at the top of trees than to the grasses below. Feeding this way opened up a layer of vegetation that shorter browsers simply could not reach, without any need for a trunk, tusks, or horns to bring the food down to its level. Height alone did the reaching that a trunk does for an elephant or a long tongue does for a giraffe today.

items.prompt: How did the giant flying bird Argentavis, among the heaviest birds ever known to fly, manage to stay airborne without exhausting itself flapping?

options.label: By flapping its wings continuously at high speed
options.feedback: A body this heavy would burn through its energy far too quickly flapping constantly; broad wings built for gliding on rising air were the better match for its size.

options.label: By riding rising currents of warm air on broad, outstretched wings
options.feedback: Broad wings held mostly still could catch columns of warm air rising off sun-heated ground, letting the bird circle upward and glide long distances while barely flapping at all.

options.label: By floating on ocean currents between short bursts of flight
options.feedback: Its skeleton points to a life spent largely over land, riding rising air rather than resting on water between flights.

options.label: By launching itself from cliffs and never flying anywhere else
options.feedback: A cliff launch would help it get airborne, but staying up for any distance depended on riding rising air currents, not on where the flight began.

items.ok_line: Wings spread wide, riding the sky's own rising air instead of fighting for lift.
items.ko_line: Think about how a large soaring bird alive today, such as a condor, stays up without flapping constantly.
items.exp_text: Ground warmed by the sun heats the air just above it, and that warmer, lighter air rises in a column that a bird can circle inside, climbing without beating its wings at all. Wings spread broad and mostly motionless caught that lift efficiently, letting a body far too heavy to sustain constant flapping stay airborne by gliding from one rising column to the next. A flight built around finding and riding this rising air let a heavy body stay aloft while spending a small fraction of the energy that continuous flapping would have demanded.
